summary: This informational note describes the eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme, a hash-based digital signature system based on existing scientific literature. It specifies WOTS+, a one-time signature scheme, XMSS as a single-tree scheme, and the multi-tree variant XMSS^MT. Such schemes are of interest because they rely on hash functions.

plainLanguage.summary: XMSS creates digital signatures using hash functions and a tree of one-time signing keys. The signer must keep track of which keys have been used and must never reuse a key state.

subtitle: A stateful digital-signature scheme built from one-time keys and hash trees.

tldr.problem: Hash-based signatures can provide digital signatures without relying on the hardness of the mathematical problems used by many other signature schemes, but the signing keys must be managed carefully.
tldr.mechanism: WOTS+ provides one-time signatures, and XMSS combines many WOTS+ keys in a Merkle tree. XMSS^MT uses multiple layers of trees.
tldr.outcome: These schemes are stateful: each signature uses a different one-time key, and reusing a key state removes the security guarantees described by the RFC.

today: RFC 8391 is an Informational document published by the IRTF in May 2018. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Hash-Based Digital Signatures
sections.content:
A digital signature lets a signer use a private key to sign a message so that others can verify it with a public key. XMSS is a hash-based signature scheme: its security relies on properties of cryptographic hash functions rather than the conjectured hardness of other mathematical problems.

The RFC specifies WOTS+, the single-tree XMSS scheme, and its multi-tree variant XMSS^MT. It describes the algorithms and formats in enough detail for implementations to interoperate. The RFC also notes that these schemes have large signatures and relatively slow key generation compared with some alternatives.
sections.plainLanguage: XMSS signs messages using hash functions and a private key. Others can check a signature with the matching public key.

sections.title: WOTS+: The One-Time Signature
sections.content:
WOTS+ is a one-time signature scheme, so a private key may sign only one message. Its private key contains starting values for a set of hash chains, and its public key contains the ends of those chains.

To sign, WOTS+ converts the message and a checksum into values that select points in the chains. A verifier continues the chains from those points and checks the resulting public-key values. Using the same private key to sign two messages makes the scheme insecure.
sections.plainLanguage: WOTS+ uses a different private key for each message. If a signer uses one of those keys twice, the scheme becomes insecure.

sections.title: XMSS: One Tree of One-Time Keys
sections.content:
XMSS places WOTS+ public keys at the leaves of a binary hash tree. Each internal node is calculated from its child nodes. The tree root and a public seed form the XMSS public key.

The private key stores an index for the next unused WOTS+ key pair. A signature contains the index, a WOTS+ signature, and an authentication path that lets the verifier recompute the root. The verifier accepts only if the computed root matches the public key. The private-key index must be updated before the signature is output.
sections.plainLanguage: XMSS combines many one-time keys under one public key. Each signature includes information that lets a verifier check its path to the public tree root.

sections.title: XMSS^MT and Parameter Choices
sections.content:
XMSS^MT arranges several XMSS trees in layers. The lowest layer signs messages; each higher layer signs the root of a tree below it. This multi-tree design addresses the slow key generation of a single large tree.

The parameters determine the hash output size, the tree height, and, for XMSS^MT, the number of layers. A tree of height h has 2^h leaves and supports that many one-time signing keys. The RFC defines required parameter sets using SHA2-256 and optional sets using other hash functions.
sections.plainLanguage: XMSS^MT uses several smaller trees linked in layers. Its parameters affect how many messages one key can sign and the size and speed of signatures.

sections.title: State Management and Security
sections.content:
XMSS and XMSS^MT are stateful: the secret key changes as signatures are produced. If a signing key state is reused, the RFC says no cryptographic security guarantees remain and a signature on a new message may be forged. Developers should use these schemes only in systems that prevent state reuse.

The signing interface must return the updated secret-key state. Restoring an old backup or copying a key without coordinating its index can reuse a one-time key. The RFC reports confidence in the schemes against quantum-computer attacks based on research available at the time, while noting that deployment experience was limited.
sections.plainLanguage: The signer must save the updated key state after every signature. If it restores an older state and reuses a key, an attacker may be able to forge a signature.
